Case Study · 002 · 2024 · MSc dissertation

Money can't buy happiness— but community can

InstitutionCity St George's, University of London ProgrammeMSc Behavioural Economics RoleSole researcher & author Duration~6 months · 2024 SupervisorDr Anke Plagnol Result71% · Distinction (MSc awarded with Merit)
In short

Across 11,249 people in five countries, social capital went with higher life satisfaction everywhere. But which kind mattered, and how much, depended on culture, natural risk and the strength of the state.

Context § 01

We usually judge how well a country is doing by its income. Yet the relationships around us, at home, at work and in our neighbourhoods, are a large part of what makes life worth living. Researchers call this social capital, and its link with life satisfaction is well established (Putnam, 2000; Helliwell & Putnam, 2004).

What is less clear is whether it works the same way everywhere. Most studies treat the link as uniform and measure trust, networks and norms with separate instruments. I used the ISSP 2017 Social Networks module, an underused survey that captures all three of Putnam's dimensions at once, and tested the link in five very different countries.

The answer: social capital matters everywhere, but not in the same way. Culture and natural risk change which relationships count. Where the state provides more, social capital carries less of the load. And the most consistent link holds in every country: people who trust that the system treats them fairly are more satisfied with life.

Overall, this is a very comprehensive study of the relationship between life satisfaction and social capital in various national contexts. It was a pleasure to read this thoughtful analysis.

— Dr Anke Plagnol · supervisor
The quote on my desk “Money can't buy happiness”: a maxim argued over since Rousseau's Discourse on the Arts and Sciences (1750). 274 years later, the data still mostly agrees.

Approach & methods § 02

The data are the ISSP 2017 Social Networks module: 11,249 respondents in five countries, analysed in R. Life satisfaction is the module's single 7-point item. Social capital is measured through 11 measures across trust, social networks, support resources, reciprocity norms and contact. 8 contextual moderators frame the comparison: what governments shape (the Human Development Index, Social Progress Index, Corruption Perceptions Index and within-country income) and what a country is given (INFORM natural-hazard risk and Hofstede's power distance, masculinity and individualism). The dissertation calls these explicit and implicit moderators.

Gaps in 3,968 of the 11,249 rows were filled by multiple imputation (MICE, predictive mean matching, grouped by country), and multi-item measures were reduced by PCA (most α ≥ 0.71). Country-level and pooled OLS with interaction terms tested four hypotheses, with estimated marginal means and Tukey comparisons between countries, VIF checks for multicollinearity and AIC/BIC to compare moderator models. Controls were age, partner status, ISCO-08 skill level and household financial ease.

Tool stack R: mice, emmeans, car (VIF). Excel for early wrangling. The ISSP codebook as gospel.
Quietly proud of Reconstructing the ISCO-08 skill levels for Chinese agricultural workers, where the ISSP module has a known missing-data issue flagged on p. 279 of its own documentation — so the Chinese sample didn't collapse.

Results § 03

The data are a snapshot, not an experiment, so every result here is an association.

H1a · Within

Social capital is positively associated with life satisfaction within each country.

Supported.

Within every country, people with more social capital reported higher life satisfaction. Trust in fairness was the most consistent link, significant in all five and strongest in Austria, more than twice the other four countries'. That fits the “warm glow” of trust in highly developed countries (Bjørnskov, 2003b).

My readingThe surprise was organisational support resources, which went with lower satisfaction, the opposite of what I expected. People may dislike having to rely on institutions for what they need. It took me a week to see it.

H1b · Between

The relationship between social capital and life satisfaction varies across countries.

Supported.

Pooling all five countries, with Austria as the baseline, shows where the same tie carried different weight. Trust in fairness was positive everywhere, but roughly half as strong outside Austria. Social networks counted for more in South Africa and daily contact for less in the United States; most other differences were not significant. Held at average social capital, these differences add up to different levels of satisfaction (Fig. 01).

H2a · Implicit

Implicit national factors — natural-disaster risk and Hofstede cultural values — moderate the relationship.

Supported, with nuance.

What a country is given changed which relationships counted. In riskier countries, trust and networks mattered less and the societal care norm more; social networks mattered more in individualistic cultures.

H2b · Explicit

Explicit national factors — human development, government resources, corruption and income — moderate the relationship.

Supported.

As the state provided more, most links weakened, while governance quality was itself linked to higher satisfaction. Relative income had no significant main effect, but household financial ease, a measure of making ends meet, was one of the strongest predictors.

Limits

Because the data are a snapshot, the arrows could point either way: satisfied people may simply invest more in community. A third factor such as personality, which the ISSP doesn't measure, could also drive both. The model explains about a fifth of the variance in life satisfaction (R² ≈ 0.22), normal for this literature. Life satisfaction is a single survey item, and China makes up 37.5% of the pooled sample (4,219 of 11,249), so pooled estimates lean towards it.

Implications The playbook § 04

Context comes first. Institutions can only do so much for wellbeing on their own, because culture and physical environment shape how people interact, so both need to be understood before anyone designs an intervention. These are directions to explore, not proven effects.

P1 · High natural-disaster risk

Plan together before the flood

Resilience may be social before it is structural.

Neighbourhood emergency plans written with residents, kept alive by street events, drills and shared meals, could build that care at a fraction of the cost of new flood defences (Table 01).

P2 · Individualistic cultures

Pubs as policy

Where people meet is already policy, whether or not anyone designs it.

Protecting community pubs and parks, designing employment resource centres as meeting points and using national sporting events to bring groups together treats those places as social infrastructure (Table 01).

P3 · Everywhere, especially advanced democracies

Fairness is infrastructure

Perceived fairness may be the one form of social capital a government can build directly.

Transparent decision-making, justice that follows through on petty crimes, fair wage distribution and easy-to-use social services make fairness visible; the dissertation also argues for progressive taxation (§ Results).

P4 · Developed societies

Community over cash

Progress could be measured in connection as well as cash.

Development projects could be judged partly by what they do for community, with community centres, clubs and mutual-aid networks funded as core development (§ Results).

What I'd do next § 05

This is a small step in a large literature. Next, I would widen the sample beyond five countries and add personality, which predicts the forms of social capital people build (Tulin, Lancee & Volker, 2018) but which the ISSP doesn't measure. I would also develop better measures of social norms. Above all, I would run a longitudinal panel, even just two waves, to separate “social capital comes first” from “satisfied people build social capital”.

These simple relationships: with family, neighbours, colleagues, friends, and broader society have the power to make life worth living.

— From the dissertation's conclusion

Modelling & inference
